newsitem.title: GERMANY: First reading of German budget ends.
newsitem.headline: First reading of German budget ends.

text.p: The four-day first reading of the German 1997 federal budget in the lower house of parliament ended on Friday and the bill will now proceed into committee discussions.
The budget, which foresees cutting total federal spending to 440 billion marks next year from 451 billion planned for this year, did not need to be voted on on Friday.
Parliamentary committees will discuss the budget spending plans in November, and parliament is likely to vote it through at the end of that month.
The lower house was due to vote later in the day on a package of austerity bills that would cut about 20 billion marks from public spending in 1997.
The federal budget cuts are one part of Bonn's wide ranging austerity package which aims to reduce the public deficit sufficiently next year to ensure qualification for the single European currency.

On Friday, parliament rejected a motion from the opposition Social Democrats that would require the government to present a supplementary budget to take into account recent projections that unemployment will stay higher than expected next year, meaning higher federal spending and lower tax revenues.
Finance Minister Theo Waigel called the motion "superfluous". He has pledged to find extra cuts during the upcoming negotiations to make sure spending does not exceed 440 billion marks.
